For lavaan the syntax always comes first. If you explicitly tell in your syntax that the factor loadings are different, then it overwrites the mimic argument. For example:

f1 =~ c(a1,a2)*y1+y2+y3

Even with mimic=mplus, the factor loading for y1 is going to be different at everry group.

But if you dont say it explicitly the mimic argument can act freely

messages.subject: Re: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
messages.subject_clean: models with identical coefficients producing radically different R^2 values
messages.body_plain:
The confusion seems to stem from the formula that is used to compute the
R^2.

R^2 of a dependent variable (say, y2), is 1 minus the (estimated)
standardized residual variance for y2. In our example:

set.seed(2002)
adf <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), x1=rnorm(100), y1=rnorm(100), y2=rnorm(100))

mod1 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1 '
mod2 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1; y1 ~ x1 '

fit1 <- sem(mod1, data=adf)
fit2 <- sem(mod2, data=adf)
summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)
summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)

For fit1, we get (see last column):

                    Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

Variances:
     y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.935

while for fit2, we get

                    Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all

Variances:
     y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.923

So we need to explain how we compute the 'Std.all' value for y2 in both
settings.

We need to compute the model-implied variances for each model, and this
is where we see the differences (see first element 'y2'):

 > diag( fitted(fit1)$cov )
        y2         x        x1        y1
0.7948851 1.0103473 0.9897522 0.8568083

 > diag( fitted(fit2)$cov )
        y2        y1         x        x1
0.8051950 0.8568084 1.0103473 0.9897522

Dividing the original estimate (0.743) by either 0.7948851 or 0.8051950
gives the two Std.all versions.

Why are the fitted variances different? Because in mod2, we have a
non-zero regression coefficient in the beta matrix (for y2 ~ x1), and
this affects the corresponding element in 'psi' matrix, and evenutally
the model implied (co)variances. Since we have no latent variables, the
model-implied covariance matrix is given by

solve(diag(4)-beta) %*% psi %*% t(  solve(diag(4)-beta) )

Both beta and psi are a bit different in the two models. but it is the
psi matrix that makes the difference.

 > inspect(fit1, "est")[3:4]
$psi
    y2     x      x1     y1
y2  0.743
x   0.000  1.010
x1  0.000 -0.035  0.990
y1  0.000  0.154  0.017  0.857

$beta
    y2     x     x1     y1
y2  0 0.181 -0.001 -0.184
x   0 0.000  0.000  0.000
x1  0 0.000  0.000  0.000
y1  0 0.000  0.000  0.000

 > inspect(fit2, "est")[3:4]
$psi
    y2     y1     x      x1
y2  0.743
y1  0.000  0.857
x   0.000  0.000  1.010
x1  0.000  0.000 -0.035  0.990

$beta
    y2     y1     x     x1
y2  0 -0.184 0.181 -0.001
y1  0  0.000 0.000  0.017
x   0  0.000 0.000  0.000
x1  0  0.000 0.000  0.000

Yves.

Right, whereas I (and I'm going to guess many other folk) are more interested in the squared multiple correlation (R^2smc in Kline p. 160) which uses the disturbance estimate divided by the observed total variance. This is often more in line with what folk are talking about when they go variable by variable, as there interested in predictive power of the equations, and it's what the function I sent gets at. Particularly when users are dealing with observed variable only models.

Hrm.

I suppose both could be reported? They should often be the same except in cases of very different model structure, yes?

Thoughts?

On Dec 2, 2013, at 7:45 AM, yrosseel <yros...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The confusion seems to stem from the formula that is used to compute the R^2.
>
> R^2 of a dependent variable (say, y2), is 1 minus the (estimated) standardized residual variance for y2. In our example:
>
> set.seed(2002)
> adf <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), x1=rnorm(100), y1=rnorm(100), y2=rnorm(100))
> mod1 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1 '
> mod2 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1; y1 ~ x1 '
> fit1 <- sem(mod1, data=adf)
> fit2 <- sem(mod2, data=adf)
> summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)
> summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)
>
> For fit1, we get (see last column):
>
>                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
> Variances:
>    y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.935
>
> while for fit2, we get
>
>                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
> Variances:
>    y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.923
>
>
> So we need to explain how we compute the 'Std.all' value for y2 in both settings.
>
> We need to compute the model-implied variances for each model, and this is where we see the differences (see first element 'y2'):
>
> > diag( fitted(fit1)$cov )
>       y2         x        x1        y1
> 0.7948851 1.0103473 0.9897522 0.8568083
>
> > diag( fitted(fit2)$cov )
>       y2        y1         x        x1
> 0.8051950 0.8568084 1.0103473 0.9897522
>
> Dividing the original estimate (0.743) by either 0.7948851 or 0.8051950 gives the two Std.all versions.
>
> Why are the fitted variances different? Because in mod2, we have a non-zero regression coefficient in the beta matrix (for y2 ~ x1), and this affects the corresponding element in 'psi' matrix, and evenutally the model implied (co)variances. Since we have no latent variables, the model-implied covariance matrix is given by

analysis with categorical variables. See the following paper for more

dichotomous variables in several groups. Psychometrika, 46, 407-419.

messages.body_plain:
Jorg--
     Yes, forcing the mean of X to 0 will affect the results, and not in a good way.  The strength of the effect depends on how far away from 0 the mean of X really is.  The farther away, the more the variance of X will be inflated, tending to weaken the calculated correlation between X and Y, thus weakening the calculated regression slope.
     You can compute the regression slope as:

B = covariance (Y,X) / variance (X)

and compute the terms on the right as:

Covariance (Y,X) = SUM [(Y - mean(Y))(X - mean(X))] / n
Variance (X) = SUM [(X - mean(X)) squared] / n

summed across all X,Y pairs

Replacing the mean of X with 0 gets you:

Covariance (Y,X) = SUM [(Y - mean(Y))(X)] / n
Variance (X) = SUM [(X) squared] / n

To see the effect, replace X with:

X = X - mean(X) + (mean(X)

in the equations above.  In the variance(X) equation, things get squared, and so replacing the actual mean of X with 0 rapidly inflates the variance, while also inflating the covariance, but not by so much.  So the denominator of the slope equation increases much more rapidly than the numerator, and the computed slope is attenuated.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: determine differences between latent means
messages.body_plain:
> How to determine differences between latent means after establishing configural, metric, and partial invariance. I have three latent variables and I want to see the difference between two groups per latent variable.
>

 I don't think the measurementInvariance function does partial automatically, so when you fit your strong invariance model, did you free the latent means in the second group?  If not, then constraining the intercepts and latent means across groups simultaneously might be why your strong invariance did not pass.

If your means are free in the second group, after establishing partial strong invariance, then your next step is to constrain the latent means across groups and conduct a chi-sq difference test to see whether that set of constraints is plausible.  To constrain all the latent means (the omnibus test), you can just add "means" to the vector of parameters to constrain in the group.equal argument.  If that test fails, then there are significant group differences in at least one of the latent means.  Instead of constraining all 3 latent means, you can fix one at a time and compare that model to the partial strong invariance model using a chi-sq difference test.  To constrain one at a time, you can either add parameters to the group.partial argument, or you can leave "means" out of the group.equal argument and manual constrain a latent mean using labels in the model syntax (e.g., "com ~ c(mean1, mean1)*com" )

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Two questions about MLR
messages.body_plain:
On 12/17/2013 01:09 PM, Chester Kam wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I wonder if you guys can answer me two questions.
>
> 1. I know of a major test for model comparison for MLR models:
> Satorra-Bentler Scaled Chi-Square Difference Test. The one being used by
> lavaan is another test - Yuan-Bentler Chi-Square Difference test, am I
> correct?

No.

If you have used MLR, it is always the Yuan-Bentler version. If you want
Satorra-Bentler, simply use estimator="MLM" for both models. But
remember that MLM only works for complete data.

Think of Yuan-Bentler as a modern version of Satorra-Bentler. There is
nothing wrong with it.

> 2. I just wonder if there is an easy way to conduct Satorra-Bentler
> Strictly Positive Scaled Chi-Square Difference Test? Editors and
> Reviewers keep asking for it, even though it is quite troublesome to
> conduct it by hand in Mplus.

Well, here is the good news: lavaan already gives you this 'strictly'
positive scaled difference test, for free. Because lavaan uses the
original Satorra (2000) formulas. You get it automatically when you are
using the anova() function on two (or more) models with scaled test
statistics.

The trouble with 'negative' values only occurs if you are using the
popular Satorra & Bentler (2001) simplification, which you can get from
lavaan if you pass the (hidden) option 'SB.classic=TRUE' to the anova
function.

In lavaan 0.5-16, there is new function lavTestLRT() (called by anova())
which contains proper documentation and references.

Yves.

impose equality constraints); not so important anymore nowadays.

messages.body_plain:
Yves,

In the parameterEstimates() function, you calculate fraction missing information using Savalei & Rhemtulla's (2012) method.  After step 2 (fitting the target model to the model-implied moments from step 1), you run a check to see whether any SEs == 0, then set those to NA before calculating FMI:

        SE.step2 <- ifelse(step2@Fit@se == 0, as.numeric(NA),
            step2@Fit@se)
        LIST$fmi <- 1 - (SE.step2^2/SE.orig^2)

I was wondering why you did this.  When would SE == 0?  If it is only approximately zero and rounds to zero even using double precision, isn't it justifiable to consider the FMI to be approximately 1 in this case?  I wouldn't expect such small SE when using truly complete data, and I don't necessarily disagree with setting it to missing in this function.  But I am running a simulation study, and I am wondering whether I should recode those NAs to 1s for my results, and my decision kind of rests on whether there is a reason you noticed that causes SEs to be 0 in step 2.

Thanks,

Terry
